## Performance Bottleneck Analysis: jlsm-core

Based on my thorough examination of jlsm-core, I've identified the **5 highest-complexity, performance-sensitive classes** that are excellent candidates for JMH benchmarking. These represent the critical hot paths in the LSM-Tree pipeline.

---

### Candidate 1: TrieSSTableWriter (SSTable Write Path)

**File:** `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/sstable/TrieSSTableWriter.java`

**Layer:** SSTable Encoding

**Benchmark Type:** Snapshot (per-operation cost)

**Hot Paths & Bottlenecks:**

- **Nested loops in `writeKeyIndex()` (lines 218-254)**: Iterates over all index keys, calls `toArray(ValueLayout.JAVA_BYTE)` for each key (line 235), then manually shifts bits to write int/long values. This is O(n * keyLen) with repeated allocations.
  
- **MemorySegment allocation in `append()` (line 131)**: `MemorySegment.ofArray(keyBytes)` for every entry added. Key arrays are cloned in lines 140-141 unnecessarily.

- **ByteBuffer write in `writeBytes()` (lines 165-171)**: Wraps encoded bytes in a ByteBuffer for I/O. For small entries, the wrapper overhead may exceed entry size.

- **DataBlock flushing (line 152)**: Checks `currentBlock.byteSize() >= SSTableFormat.DEFAULT_BLOCK_SIZE` on every append—the block must serialize all entries again on flush (line 160).

- **Bloom filter construction (lines 186-189)**: Iterates over indexKeys twice (once to create filter, once to add keys). The factory is invoked at finish time with accumulated keys.

**GC Pressure:** High—temporary byte arrays for keys, MemorySegments created per entry, repeated ArrayList allocations in nested loops.

**Recommended Benchmark:**
- Append 100K–1M sorted entries of varying key/value sizes
- Measure time to reach finish()
- Track allocation rate and GC pauses
- Vary block size and entry size distributions

---

### Candidate 2: BlockedBloomFilter (Probabilistic Lookup)

**File:** `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/bloom/blocked/BlockedBloomFilter.java`

**Layer:** Block Encoding (Cache-Friendly Hashing)

**Benchmark Type:** Snapshot (per-operation: `add()` and `mightContain()`)

**Hot Paths & Bottlenecks:**

- **Hash computation (lines 118, 141)**: `Murmur3Hash.hash128(key)` is called for every add/lookup. Two hash function calls per entry = expensive.

- **Double-hash loop (lines 129-133, 151-157)**: For each operation, loop k times (1–30 iterations, typically ~8–10) to probe bits. Each iteration:
  - Computes `bitPos = (h1 + (long) i * h2) & 511`
  - Reads/writes `bits[blockBase + (bitPos >>> 6)]` via array indexing
  - These are single-instruction operations but loop overhead is non-negligible at k=30.

- **Block modulo operation (line 125, 147)**: `(h1 & Long.MAX_VALUE) % numBlocks`—modulo is slower than bit masks; scaling to 1M+ entries means 1M+ modulo operations.

- **Serialization (lines 194-206)**: Iterates over all bits (numBlocks * 8 longs), writes each via FFM ValueLayout. This is O(m) where m = total bits, can be millions.

**Specialized Cost:** The `| 1L` forcing h2 odd (line 123, 145) is intentional and required; its absence would cause 6× FPR inflation per the comment.

**Recommended Benchmark:**
- `add()` 10K–100K keys of varying length
- `mightContain()` for 1K keys (hits + misses)
- Measure cache misses (LLC misses via perf) to validate cache-line locality claim
- Vary number of blocks to observe scaling
- Profile Murmur3Hash cost in isolation

---

### Candidate 3: SpookyCompactor & MergeIterator (Compaction Merge)

**File:** `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/compaction/SpookyCompactor.java` and `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/compaction/internal/MergeIterator.java`

**Layer:** Compaction (Merge-Sort Pipeline)

**Benchmark Type:** Sustained (accumulation over dataset size)

**Hot Paths & Bottlenecks:**

- **N-way merge heap (MergeIterator, lines 50-59)**: Every `next()` call does:
  - `heap.poll()` — O(log n) where n = number of input iterators (typically 2–10 SSTables)
  - `heap.offer()` with new HeapEntry — O(log n)
  - These are triggered once per entry, so total merge cost is O(E log n) where E = total entries.

- **Nested loops in `selectCompaction()` (lines 84-98)**: For each bottom-level file, scan ALL upper-level files to find overlaps. O(B × U) where B = bottom files, U = upper files. Can be O(n²) in pathological cases.

- **Key comparison in HEAP_ORDER (lines 23-28)**: Comparator calls `KeyRangeUtil.compareUnsigned()` twice per heap operation—20+ invocations per merged entry in a 10-way merge.

- **Entry iteration in `writeMergedOutput()` (lines 179-209)**: Dedup check `KeyRangeUtil.keysEqual()` on every entry (line 183). Grow output file list if exceeds `targetBottomFileSizeBytes` (line 204).

- **Multiple SSTable opens (lines 143-147)**: Eager open of all source SSTables—loads entire data regions into memory before merge begins. No streaming; high memory footprint.

**Resource Growth:** As compaction level increases, number of SSTables per level grows; deeper levels mean larger merge operations and slower progress.

**Recommended Benchmark:**
- Compact 2–10 SSTables, varying entry counts (10K–1M per SSTable)
- Measure throughput (entries/sec) and memory peak
- Profile key comparison cost and heap operations
- Vary data locality (overlapping ranges vs. disjoint ranges)
- Test with deep level hierarchies (L0→L5)

---

### Candidate 4: TrieSSTableReader (SSTable Read Path)

**File:** `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/sstable/TrieSSTableReader.java`

**Layer:** SSTable Decoding

**Benchmark Type:** Snapshot & Sustained (point lookups + range scans)

**Hot Paths & Bottlenecks:**

- **Eager full-data load in `open()` (lines 92-94)**: Reads entire data region into a single byte array. For large SSTables (GiB+), this is a GC-triggering allocation. No lazy alternative in eager mode.

- **Bloom filter lookup (line 143)**: Every `get()` must call `bloomFilter.mightContain(key)` before index lookup. False positives lead to wasted index lookups.

- **KeyIndex.lookup() (line 147)**: Trie tree traversal, O(|key|) with binary search at each node. Deserialization on lookup: key bytes are materialized via `toArray()` in KeyIndex (internal, lines 156, 201).

- **readDataAt() with cache (lines 191-214)**: Checks block cache, falls through to read if miss. Cache misses trigger `System.arraycopy()` from eagerData or lazy channel read. No cache hit optimization avoids the copy.

- **DataRegionIterator (lines 329-383)**: Advances through data blocks, parsing entries per block:
  - Line 353: `readInt(data, offset)` to get block count
  - Line 355: `new ArrayList<>(count)` pre-allocation per block
  - Line 357: Decode each entry and add to list—O(block size) memory allocation per block iteration.

- **KeyIndex byte conversion (lines 250-264)**: On construction, materializes all key bytes from index buffer via `System.arraycopy()`. Creates n MemorySegments, one per key.

**GC Pressure:** High from eager load, ArrayList allocations per block, and cache misses triggering copies.

**Recommended Benchmark:**
- Point lookups: 10K–1M keys with varying Bloom filter FPRs
- Range scans: 100K–1M entries per SSTable
- Measure cache hit rate vs. memory peak
- Compare eager vs. lazy load under memory pressure
- Profile iterator advancement cost

---

### Candidate 5: LocalWriteAheadLog (WAL Write + Recovery)

**File:** `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/wal/local/LocalWriteAheadLog.java`

**Layer:** Write-Ahead Log (Durability)

**Benchmark Type:** Snapshot (per-append cost) & Sustained (recovery time)

**Hot Paths & Bottlenecks:**

- **Per-append write path (lines 200-230)**:
  - Line 210: `bufferPool.acquire()` — blocking queue poll with timeout
  - Line 212: `WalRecord.encode()` — serializes entry into buffer
  - Line 218: `MemorySegment.copy()` from buffer to mapped region
  - Line 221: `mappedBuffer.force(writePosition - n, n)` — **fsync for durability** (most expensive)
  - These execute under `writeLock`, serializing all appends.

- **Roll segment on overflow (lines 232-253)**: 
  - Lines 236–237: Force and truncate current segment
  - Line 244: Create new segment file (pre-allocates 64 MiB via sparse write, line 189)
  - Lock contention on indexLock during roll.

- **Recovery scan (lines 79-121)**: 
  - Iterates all segments, decoding records for each (line 97)
  - `scanSegment()` reads entire segment via mmap, loops through all records (lines 141–162)
  - CRC mismatch handling stops at first corrupt record (line 147)—no resilience for partial writes.

- **ReplayIterator (lines 381-471)**: 
  - Line 428: `FileChannel.open()` per segment
  - Line 429: `map()` segment file to read-only buffer
  - Line 443: Decode each record with CRC check—O(record size) per record.

- **Segment index operations (lines 276-307)**: 
  - Build segmentsForReplay iterates segmentIndex to find start (O(n) scan)
  - Read lock held during iteration, no fast path for small WAL.

**Contention:** `writeLock` serializes all appends—no write parallelism. fsync dominates latency (10–100 ms).

**Recommended Benchmark:**
- Append throughput: 1K–100K entries, varying WAL record sizes
- Measure fsync latency per append (critical!)
- Replay performance: 10K–1M entries, varying segment counts
- Recovery time with corrupted records (CRC mismatches)
- Compare local vs. remote WAL (RemoteWriteAheadLog) for same workload

---

### Summary Table

| Candidate | Class | File Path | Layer | Bench Type | Key Bottleneck | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | TrieSSTableWriter | `/jlsm/sstable/TrieSSTableWriter.java` | SSTable | Snapshot | Nested loops + repeated MemorySegment alloc | HIGH |
| 2 | BlockedBloomFilter | `/jlsm/bloom/blocked/BlockedBloomFilter.java` | Encoding | Snapshot | Hash + double-hash loop + modulo | HIGH |
| 3 | SpookyCompactor + MergeIterator | `/jlsm/compaction/SpookyCompactor.java`, `/jlsm/compaction/internal/MergeIterator.java` | Compaction | Sustained | N-way merge heap + nested overlap scan | CRITICAL |
| 4 | TrieSSTableReader | `/jlsm/sstable/TrieSSTableReader.java` | SSTable | Snapshot + Sustained | Eager load + cache + iterator | HIGH |
| 5 | LocalWriteAheadLog | `/jlsm/wal/local/LocalWriteAheadLog.java` | WAL | Snapshot + Sustained | fsync latency + lock contention + recovery | CRITICAL |

---

### Honorable Mentions (Secondary Candidates)

- **LruBlockCache** (`/jlsm/cache/LruBlockCache.java`): Single ReentrantLock on every get/put—all operations are serialized. Linked­HashMap access-order eviction modifies internal state per get. Good for lock contention analysis.

- **KeyIndex (Trie)** (`/jlsm/sstable/internal/KeyIndex.java`): Trie construction inserts one key at a time with binary search + array copies in Inner.put() (lines 52-69). O(n * |key| * log(branching)) construction cost. Good for scaling studies.

- **ConcurrentSkipListMemTable** (`/jlsm/memtable/ConcurrentSkipListMemTable.java`): MemTable uses ConcurrentSkipListMap; concurrent reads + writes. AtomicLong size tracking with addAndGet(). Good for concurrent write scaling analysis.

These three are lower-priority but useful for understanding trade-offs and scaling characteristics.

## Performance Bottleneck Analysis: jlsm-core

Based on my thorough examination of jlsm-core, I've identified the **5 highest-complexity, performance-sensitive classes** that are excellent candidates for JMH benchmarking. These represent the critical hot paths in the LSM-Tree pipeline.

### Candidate 1: TrieSSTableWriter (SSTable Write Path)

**File:** `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/sstable/TrieSSTableWriter.java`

**Layer:** SSTable Encoding

**Benchmark Type:** Snapshot (per-operation cost)

**Hot Paths & Bottlenecks:**

- **Nested loops in `writeKeyIndex()` (lines 218-254)**: Iterates over all index keys, calls `toArray(ValueLayout.JAVA_BYTE)` for each key (line 235), then manually shifts bits to write int/long values. This is O(n * keyLen) with repeated allocations.
  
- **MemorySegment allocation in `append()` (line 131)**: `MemorySegment.ofArray(keyBytes)` for every entry added. Key arrays are cloned in lines 140-141 unnecessarily.

- **ByteBuffer write in `writeBytes()` (lines 165-171)**: Wraps encoded bytes in a ByteBuffer for I/O. For small entries, the wrapper overhead may exceed entry size.

- **DataBlock flushing (line 152)**: Checks `currentBlock.byteSize() >= SSTableFormat.DEFAULT_BLOCK_SIZE` on every append—the block must serialize all entries again on flush (line 160).

- **Bloom filter construction (lines 186-189)**: Iterates over indexKeys twice (once to create filter, once to add keys). The factory is invoked at finish time with accumulated keys.

**GC Pressure:** High—temporary byte arrays for keys, MemorySegments created per entry, repeated ArrayList allocations in nested loops.

**Recommended Benchmark:**
- Append 100K–1M sorted entries of varying key/value sizes
- Measure time to reach finish()
- Track allocation rate and GC pauses
- Vary block size and entry size distributions

---

### Candidate 2: BlockedBloomFilter (Probabilistic Lookup)

**File:** `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/bloom/blocked/BlockedBloomFilter.java`

**Layer:** Block Encoding (Cache-Friendly Hashing)

**Benchmark Type:** Snapshot (per-operation: `add()` and `mightContain()`)

**Hot Paths & Bottlenecks:**

- **Hash computation (lines 118, 141)**: `Murmur3Hash.hash128(key)` is called for every add/lookup. Two hash function calls per entry = expensive.

- **Double-hash loop (lines 129-133, 151-157)**: For each operation, loop k times (1–30 iterations, typically ~8–10) to probe bits. Each iteration:
  - Computes `bitPos = (h1 + (long) i * h2) & 511`
  - Reads/writes `bits[blockBase + (bitPos >>> 6)]` via array indexing
  - These are single-instruction operations but loop overhead is non-negligible at k=30.

- **Block modulo operation (line 125, 147)**: `(h1 & Long.MAX_VALUE) % numBlocks`—modulo is slower than bit masks; scaling to 1M+ entries means 1M+ modulo operations.

- **Serialization (lines 194-206)**: Iterates over all bits (numBlocks * 8 longs), writes each via FFM ValueLayout. This is O(m) where m = total bits, can be millions.

**Specialized Cost:** The `| 1L` forcing h2 odd (line 123, 145) is intentional and required; its absence would cause 6× FPR inflation per the comment.

**Recommended Benchmark:**
- `add()` 10K–100K keys of varying length
- `mightContain()` for 1K keys (hits + misses)
- Measure cache misses (LLC misses via perf) to validate cache-line locality claim
- Vary number of blocks to observe scaling
- Profile Murmur3Hash cost in isolation

---

### Candidate 3: SpookyCompactor & MergeIterator (Compaction Merge)

**File:** `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/compaction/SpookyCompactor.java` and `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/compaction/internal/MergeIterator.java`

**Layer:** Compaction (Merge-Sort Pipeline)

**Benchmark Type:** Sustained (accumulation over dataset size)

**Hot Paths & Bottlenecks:**

- **N-way merge heap (MergeIterator, lines 50-59)**: Every `next()` call does:
  - `heap.poll()` — O(log n) where n = number of input iterators (typically 2–10 SSTables)
  - `heap.offer()` with new HeapEntry — O(log n)
  - These are triggered once per entry, so total merge cost is O(E log n) where E = total entries.

- **Nested loops in `selectCompaction()` (lines 84-98)**: For each bottom-level file, scan ALL upper-level files to find overlaps. O(B × U) where B = bottom files, U = upper files. Can be O(n²) in pathological cases.

- **Key comparison in HEAP_ORDER (lines 23-28)**: Comparator calls `KeyRangeUtil.compareUnsigned()` twice per heap operation—20+ invocations per merged entry in a 10-way merge.

- **Entry iteration in `writeMergedOutput()` (lines 179-209)**: Dedup check `KeyRangeUtil.keysEqual()` on every entry (line 183). Grow output file list if exceeds `targetBottomFileSizeBytes` (line 204).

- **Multiple SSTable opens (lines 143-147)**: Eager open of all source SSTables—loads entire data regions into memory before merge begins. No streaming; high memory footprint.

**Resource Growth:** As compaction level increases, number of SSTables per level grows; deeper levels mean larger merge operations and slower progress.

**Recommended Benchmark:**
- Compact 2–10 SSTables, varying entry counts (10K–1M per SSTable)
- Measure throughput (entries/sec) and memory peak
- Profile key comparison cost and heap operations
- Vary data locality (overlapping ranges vs. disjoint ranges)
- Test with deep level hierarchies (L0→L5)

### Candidate 4: TrieSSTableReader (SSTable Read Path)

**File:** `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/sstable/TrieSSTableReader.java`

**Layer:** SSTable Decoding

**Benchmark Type:** Snapshot & Sustained (point lookups + range scans)

**Hot Paths & Bottlenecks:**

- **Eager full-data load in `open()` (lines 92-94)**: Reads entire data region into a single byte array. For large SSTables (GiB+), this is a GC-triggering allocation. No lazy alternative in eager mode.

- **Bloom filter lookup (line 143)**: Every `get()` must call `bloomFilter.mightContain(key)` before index lookup. False positives lead to wasted index lookups.

- **KeyIndex.lookup() (line 147)**: Trie tree traversal, O(|key|) with binary search at each node. Deserialization on lookup: key bytes are materialized via `toArray()` in KeyIndex (internal, lines 156, 201).

- **readDataAt() with cache (lines 191-214)**: Checks block cache, falls through to read if miss. Cache misses trigger `System.arraycopy()` from eagerData or lazy channel read. No cache hit optimization avoids the copy.

- **DataRegionIterator (lines 329-383)**: Advances through data blocks, parsing entries per block:
  - Line 353: `readInt(data, offset)` to get block count
  - Line 355: `new ArrayList<>(count)` pre-allocation per block
  - Line 357: Decode each entry and add to list—O(block size) memory allocation per block iteration.

- **KeyIndex byte conversion (lines 250-264)**: On construction, materializes all key bytes from index buffer via `System.arraycopy()`. Creates n MemorySegments, one per key.

**GC Pressure:** High from eager load, ArrayList allocations per block, and cache misses triggering copies.

**Recommended Benchmark:**
- Point lookups: 10K–1M keys with varying Bloom filter FPRs
- Range scans: 100K–1M entries per SSTable
- Measure cache hit rate vs. memory peak
- Compare eager vs. lazy load under memory pressure

### Candidate 5: LocalWriteAheadLog (WAL Write + Recovery)

**File:** `/home/user/Code/github/nathauser/jlsm/modules/jlsm-core/src/main/java/jlsm/wal/local/LocalWriteAheadLog.java`

**Layer:** Write-Ahead Log (Durability)

**Benchmark Type:** Snapshot (per-append cost) & Sustained (recovery time)

**Hot Paths & Bottlenecks:**

- **Per-append write path (lines 200-230)**:
  - Line 210: `bufferPool.acquire()` — blocking queue poll with timeout
  - Line 212: `WalRecord.encode()` — serializes entry into buffer
  - Line 218: `MemorySegment.copy()` from buffer to mapped region
  - Line 221: `mappedBuffer.force(writePosition - n, n)` — **fsync for durability** (most expensive)
  - These execute under `writeLock`, serializing all appends.

- **Roll segment on overflow (lines 232-253)**: 
  - Lines 236–237: Force and truncate current segment
  - Line 244: Create new segment file (pre-allocates 64 MiB via sparse write, line 189)
  - Lock contention on indexLock during roll.

- **Recovery scan (lines 79-121)**: 
  - Iterates all segments, decoding records for each (line 97)
  - `scanSegment()` reads entire segment via mmap, loops through all records (lines 141–162)
  - CRC mismatch handling stops at first corrupt record (line 147)—no resilience for partial writes.

  - Line 429: `map()` segment file to read-only buffer
  - Line 443: Decode each record with CRC check—O(record size) per record.

- **Segment index operations (lines 276-307)**: 
  - Build segmentsForReplay iterates segmentIndex to find start (O(n) scan)
  - Read lock held during iteration, no fast path for small WAL.

**Contention:** `writeLock` serializes all appends—no write parallelism. fsync dominates latency (10–100 ms).

content.text:
Now I have a clear picture. Here's the analysis:

---

## Analysis Results — MemTable Snapshot

### Throughput summary

| Benchmark | 1K entries | 10K entries | 100K entries | Scaling |
|-----------|-----------|------------|-------------|---------|
| **getHit** | 2.31M ops/s | 1.81M ops/s | 1.19M ops/s | ~2x degradation 1K→100K |
| **getMiss** | 1.74M ops/s | 1.43M ops/s | 1.39M ops/s | ~20% degradation (nearly flat at 10K+) |
| **put** | 156K ops/s | 201K ops/s | 254K ops/s | *Inverted* — throughput increases with size |

### Key observations

**1. `put` is 6-10x slower than `get`** — and it gets *worse* at small sizes, not large ones. The profiler explains why:

**2. The `assert` in `apply()` is the dominant cost of `put`.** Line 54: `assert map.containsKey(compositeKey)`. This calls `ConcurrentSkipListMap.containsKey()` → `doGet()` → full skip list traversal with `KeyComparator.compare()` on every single put. The profiler shows:
- `ConcurrentSkipListMap.doPut`: 75+67+48+17+17+16 = **240 samples**
- `ConcurrentSkipListMap.containsKey` (from the assert): 44+32+30+19+18+15+15 = **173 samples**

The assert is doing a **full get() after every put()** — that's nearly doubling the cost. At small sizes (1K), the skip list is shallow so the assert traversal is relatively cheaper, but the overhead is still ~42% of total put CPU.

**3. `KeyComparator.compare` → `MemorySegment.mismatch` is the hottest application frame** at 1363 total samples. The call chain is:
- `KeyComparator.compare` → `AbstractMemorySegmentImpl.mismatch` → `SegmentBulkOperations.mismatch` → `HeapMemorySegmentImpl$OfByte.unsafeGetBase`
- This is the inner loop of every skip list navigation — both for `doPut` and the `containsKey` assert.

**4. G1 GC is consuming significant CPU** — ~640 samples in G1 evacuation/marking/rebuild threads. The `put` benchmark creates `new SequenceNumber()`, `new CompositeKey()`, and `new Entry.Put()` per operation, all short-lived objects putting pressure on young gen.

**5. `getHit` scales as expected** — O(log n) degradation with skip list size. 2.31M→1.19M from 1K→100K entries is consistent with skip list depth growth (log₂(100K)/log₂(1K) ≈ 1.7x expected, observed 1.9x — slightly worse due to cache pressure at larger sizes).

**6. `getMiss` is nearly flat after 10K** — once the skip list is deep enough, the ceiling lookup short-circuits early when it finds a key that lexicographically exceeds the "zzz-" prefix.

---

## Finding: Assert in apply() doubles put cost

- **Location:** `jlsm.memtable.ConcurrentSkipListMemTable#apply` line 54
- **Layer:** MemTable
- **Run mode:** Snapshot
- **Tier:** Scratch
- **Status:** Confirmed
- **Hypothesis:** The `assert map.containsKey(compositeKey)` performs a full O(log n) skip list lookup after every put, nearly doubling the per-operation cost
- **Evidence:** Profiler shows 173 samples in `containsKey`→`doGet` path vs 240 in `doPut` path (42% overhead). Put throughput is 6-10x slower than get.
- **Proposed fix:** Remove or weaken the assert. Options:
  1. Remove entirely — `ConcurrentSkipListMap.put` is well-tested JDK code, the post-condition is guaranteed
  2. Replace with a debug-only check gated on a system property
  3. Use the return value of `map.put()` (it returns the previous value) to assert on instead — zero extra traversal
- **Impact:** High — this is the write path, every single mutation pays this cost
- **Benchmark to validate:** `./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmhProfile -Pprofile "-Pjmh.includes=MemTableScratch"`
- **Detected on commit:** 543f0e3

---

## Finding: MemorySegment.mismatch dominates key comparison

- **Location:** `jlsm.memtable.internal.KeyComparator#compare` → `MemorySegment.mismatch`
- **Layer:** MemTable
- **Run mode:** Snapshot
- **Tier:** Scratch
- **Status:** Open
- **Hypothesis:** `MemorySegment.mismatch()` on heap-backed segments goes through `SegmentBulkOperations.mismatch` → `HeapMemorySegmentImpl.unsafeGetBase`, which has scoped memory access overhead. For short keys (12 bytes like "key-00000001"), the per-call overhead may exceed the actual comparison work.
- **Evidence:** 1363 total samples in `KeyComparator.compare`, 707 in `SegmentBulkOperations.mismatch`. Top leaf frames are `unsafeGetBase` (72 samples) and `getIntUnaligned` (19 samples) — suggesting the FFM boundary-checking is significant relative to the actual byte comparison.
- **Proposed fix:** For short keys, a direct byte-by-byte comparison or `Arrays.mismatch` on the backing `byte[]` (bypassing FFM overhead) could be faster. Needs a scratch benchmark isolating mismatch overhead vs raw comparison.
- **Impact:** Medium — this is the inner loop of all skip list operations, but the overhead is inherent to the FFM API design
- **Benchmark to validate:** Isolate `KeyComparator.compare` in a micro-benchmark comparing `MemorySegment.mismatch` vs `Arrays.mismatch` for varying key lengths
- **Detected on commit:** 543f0e3

---

Now cleaning up the scratch benchmark and output.

```bash
# Allocation profile (sustained):

./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmhProfile \
  -Pprofile -PprofileEvent=alloc -PrunMode=sustained -Pjfr -PgcLog \
  "-Pjmh.includes=<Name>"
```

- `--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector`

# jlsm Performance Context

> This file is maintained by the perf-review agent. Updated at the end of
> every session via `/perf-review --close`. Do not edit manually unless
> correcting an error.

---

## Gradle JMH invocations

Plugin: `me.champeau.jmh` v0.7.2, JMH 1.37
Shared config: `benchmarks/jmh-common.gradle` (applied by all benchmark modules)

### Benchmark modules

| Module | Gradle task | Purpose |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| `jlsm-bloom-benchmarks` | `:benchmarks:jlsm-bloom-benchmarks:jmh` | Bloom filter benchmarks |
| `jlsm-tree-benchmarks` | `:benchmarks:jlsm-tree-benchmarks:jmh` | LSM tree benchmarks |
| `jlsm-perf-scratch` | `:benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmh` | Scratch benchmarks (sources from `perf-scratch/`) |

### Commands

```bash
# ── Snapshot run (default) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# fork=2, warmup=3x1s, measure=5x2s
./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmh "-Pjmh.includes=<Name>Scratch"

# ── Sustained run ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# fork=1, warmup=5x5s, measure=30x5s (state accumulates across iterations)
./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmh "-Pjmh.includes=<Name>Scratch" -PrunMode=sustained

# ── With async-profiler (collapsed stacks) ───────────────────────────────
# CPU profile (snapshot):
./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmhProfile -Pprofile "-Pjmh.includes=<Name>"
# Allocation profile (sustained):
./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmhProfile -Pprofile -PprofileEvent=alloc -PrunMode=sustained "-Pjmh.includes=<Name>"

# ── With JFR recording (sustained only) ─────────────────────────────────
./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmh -PrunMode=sustained -Pjfr "-Pjmh.includes=<Name>"

# ── With GC text log (sustained only) ───────────────────────────────────
./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmh -PrunMode=sustained -PgcLog "-Pjmh.includes=<Name>"

# ── Full sustained analysis (all profiling enabled) ─────────────────────
./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmhProfile \
  -Pprofile -PprofileEvent=alloc -PrunMode=sustained -Pjfr -PgcLog \
  "-Pjmh.includes=<Name>"
```

### Output routing

All results go to `perf-output/<module-name>/`:
- `results.json` — JMH JSON with per-iteration `rawData` arrays
- `profiler.collapsed` — CPU collapsed stacks (snapshot, `-Pprofile`)
- `alloc.collapsed` — allocation collapsed stacks (sustained, `-Pprofile -PprofileEvent=alloc`)
- `recording.jfr` — JFR recording (sustained, `-Pjfr`)
- `gc.log` — GC text log (sustained, `-PgcLog`)

### JVM flags (always applied)

- `-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+DebugNonSafepoints` — line-level profiler accuracy
- `-ea` — assertions enabled in benchmarked code
- `--add-exports` for all internal packages (jlsm-core, jlsm-table)
- `--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector`

### Run mode defaults

| Mode | Fork | Warmup | Measurement |
|------|------|--------|-------------|
| Snapshot (default) | 2 | 3x1s | 5x2s |
| Sustained (`-PrunMode=sustained`) | 1 | 5x5s | 30x5s |
| With profiler (`-Pprofile`) | 1 (override) | — | — |

content.text:
Here's the analysis:

---

## Analysis Results — SSTable Write Snapshot

### Throughput

| entryCount | ops/s | per-entry time |
|------------|-------|----------------|
| 1,000 | 125.5 | ~8.0 μs/entry |
| 10,000 | 44.7 | ~2.2 μs/entry |

Per-entry time drops 3.6x from 1K→10K, meaning the fixed cost of `finish()` (bloom filter, key index, fsync) dominates at low entry counts.

### Profiler breakdown (application frames)

| Component | Samples | % of app | Layer |
|-----------|---------|----------|-------|
| **I/O: channel.write** | 650 | 35% | SSTable I/O |
| **append()** total | 457 | 25% | SSTable encoding |
| **toArray()** (MemorySegment→byte[]) | 347 | 19% | GC pressure / encoding |
| **finish()** total | 332 | 18% | SSTable finalization |
| **flushCurrentBlock()** | 322 | 17% | SSTable I/O |
| **writeKeyIndex()** | 80 | 4% | SSTable encoding |
| **BloomFilter.add** | 82 | 4% | Bloom filter |
| **Murmur3Hash.hash128** | 74 | 4% | Bloom filter |
| **EntryCodec.encode** | 57 | 3% | SSTable encoding |
| **BloomFilter.serialize** | 14 | 1% | Bloom filter |
| **DataBlock.serialize** | 11 | 1% | SSTable encoding |

### Key findings

**1. I/O dominates (35%)** — `FileChannel.write` → `UnixFileDispatcherImpl.write0` is the single largest cost. This is expected for a write-path benchmark. The `ByteBuffer.wrap()` per block flush is lightweight; the actual syscall is the bottleneck.

**2. `toArray()` is the biggest CPU-side waste (19%)** — `MemorySegment.toArray(JAVA_BYTE)` appears 347 times. This happens **3 times per entry**:
   - Once in `TrieSSTableWriter.append()` line 113: `entry.key().toArray()`
   - Once in `EntryCodec.encode()` line 56: `entry.key().toArray()` (redundant!)
   - Once in `EntryCodec.encode()` line 63: `put.value().toArray()`
   
   Plus once more per key in `writeKeyIndex()` line 235: `indexKeys.get(i).toArray()` — but `indexKeys` already stores `MemorySegment.ofArray(keyBytes)`, so this round-trips byte[]→MemorySegment→byte[].

**3. Bloom filter construction is cheap (8% total)** — `add` + `hash128` together are ~8%. This is well-optimized.

**4. DataBlock serialization is negligible (1%)** — the `System.arraycopy` in `DataBlock.serialize()` is fast.

**5. C2 JIT compilation is significant (320 samples)** — expected for fork=1 with short runs. Not a real concern for production.

---

## Finding: Redundant toArray allocations in SSTable write path

- **Location:** `jlsm.sstable.TrieSSTableWriter#append` + `jlsm.sstable.internal.EntryCodec#encode`
- **Layer:** SSTable encoding / GC pressure
- **Run mode:** Snapshot
- **Tier:** Scratch
- **Status:** Confirmed
- **Hypothesis:** Each entry appended to an SSTable triggers 3+ `MemorySegment.toArray()` calls, each allocating a new byte[]. The key bytes are extracted in `append()` (line 113), then extracted again in `EntryCodec.encode()` (line 56). The key is then stored as `MemorySegment.ofArray(keyBytes)` in `indexKeys`, only to be extracted a third time in `writeKeyIndex()` (line 235). This is ~19% of total CPU.
- **Evidence:** 347 profiler samples in `AbstractMemorySegmentImpl.toArray`. Three distinct call sites extracting the same key bytes.
- **Proposed fix:**
  1. Change `append()` to extract key bytes once and pass them to `EntryCodec.encode(entry, keyBytes)` overload
  2. Store raw `byte[]` in `indexKeys` instead of `MemorySegment` — eliminates the round-trip in `writeKeyIndex()`
  3. Store the extracted key bytes for the ordering check (`lastKeyBytes`) directly — already done, but the `MemorySegment.ofArray(keyBytes)` for indexKeys is redundant
- **Impact:** Medium — reduces per-entry allocations from 3+ to 1 for keys, saving ~19% CPU and GC pressure
- **Benchmark to validate:** `./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmhProfile -Pprofile "-Pjmh.includes=SSTableWriteScratch"`
- **Detected on commit:** 543f0e3

## Finding: I/O is the dominant cost in SSTable writes

- **Location:** `jlsm.sstable.TrieSSTableWriter#writeBytes` → `FileChannel.write`
- **Layer:** SSTable I/O
- **Run mode:** Snapshot
- **Tier:** Scratch
- **Status:** Open — investigated, expected behavior
- **Hypothesis:** `FileChannel.write` syscalls consume 35% of total CPU. This is the floor — real I/O cost will be higher on disk-bound systems.
- **Evidence:** 650 samples in `IOUtil.write` chain down to `write0` native call
- **Proposed fix:** Consider batching multiple blocks into a single write call, or writing all blocks to a pre-allocated buffer and flushing once at `finish()`. However, this trades memory for I/O batching and may not be worthwhile for the current block-at-a-time design.
- **Impact:** Low — this is inherent to the write path; optimizing above I/O is more productive
- **Detected on commit:** 543f0e3

---

Scratch benchmark and output cleaned up. Two new findings recorded.

**Summary so far this session:**
- **4 findings total** — 1 fixed (MemTable assert), 2 confirmed (toArray redundancy, MemorySegment.mismatch overhead), 1 open/expected (I/O cost)
- **1 regression benchmark promoted** (MemTableBenchmark)
- **2 components explored** (MemTable, SSTable write)

What's next? The remaining high-priority targets from the exploration:
- **SSTable read** (`TrieSSTableReader`) — point lookup path
- **Compaction merge** (`SpookyCompactor` + `MergeIterator`) — sustained candidate
- **WAL** (`LocalWriteAheadLog`) — fsync latency

Or type `wrap up` to close the session and persist all findings.

For the current session where I'm operating as the general agent, you'd need to approve them in your settings or approve once and select "always allow".

---

## Analysis Results — Three Components

### 1. SSTable Read (TrieSSTableReader)

| Benchmark | Score | Notes |
|-----------|-------|-------|
| **getHit** | 1.07M ops/s | Point lookup of existing key |
| **getMiss** | 12.85M ops/s | Bloom filter rejects — 12x faster than hit |
| **fullScan** | 1,277 ops/s | Full 10K-entry scan per op |

**Profiler breakdown:**
- `BloomFilter.mightContain` → `Murmur3Hash.hash128`: 723+461 = **1,184 samples** (dominant for both hit and miss paths)
- `toArray()`: **708 samples** — `readDataAt()` returns byte[] via arraycopy from eagerData, then `EntryCodec.decode` allocates more byte arrays
- `KeyIndex.lookup`: only **10 samples** — trie lookup is fast, not a bottleneck

**Finding:** Bloom filter hash is the dominant cost of point lookups. For hits, the bloom check is wasted work (it always passes). For misses, it's the entire cost — and it's fast (12.85M ops/s). The real optimization target for reads is the `toArray` / decode path after the bloom check confirms a hit.

### 2. Compaction Merge (SpookyCompactor)

| Benchmark | 2 SSTables | 4 SSTables |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| **compactOverlapping** | 46.7 ops/s | 34.4 ops/s |

Per-entry: ~4.3μs (2-way), ~5.8μs (4-way). 35% degradation going 2→4 way.

**Profiler breakdown:**
- `TrieSSTableReader.open` (eager read): **868 samples** — dominates! Reading source SSTables is the biggest cost
- `writeMergedOutput`: **526 samples** — the actual merge loop
- `readKeyIndex` + `KeyIndex.init/insert`: **211+192+167 = 570 samples** — trie construction on open
- `MergeIterator.next`: **160 samples** — heap operations, less than expected
- `TrieSSTableWriter.append/finish`: **188+166 = 354 samples** — output writing
- `toArray`: **154 samples**

**Finding:** Compaction is dominated by **SSTable open I/O** (868 samples), not the merge itself (160 samples). The eager `open()` reads the entire data region into memory for each source SSTable before the merge begins. For compaction, a lazy/streaming approach would eliminate this upfront cost.

### 3. WAL Append (LocalWriteAheadLog)

| Benchmark | 128B value | 1024B value |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| **append** | 427 ops/s | 321 ops/s |

That's **~2.3ms per append** at 128B, **~3.1ms per append** at 1024B.

**Profiler breakdown:**
- `MappedByteBuffer.force()` chain: 37+37+36+36+35+34 = **~72 samples** (from only 72 total in `append`) — **virtually 100% of append time is fsync**
- `MemorySegment.copy`: **21 samples** — the actual data write
- `WalRecord.encode`: **13 samples** — encoding is cheap
- `ArenaBufferPool.acquire/release`: **3 samples** — negligible
- `writeLock`: not visible in profiler — no contention (single-threaded benchmark)

**Finding:** WAL append is completely dominated by `mappedBuffer.force()` — this is the fsync call that guarantees durability. At ~2-3ms per fsync, this is the expected latency for a single-record fsync on Linux. This is not a code bug — it's the fundamental cost of durability. The only way to improve throughput is group commit (batch multiple appends before fsync).

---

## New Findings Summary

### Finding: Bloom filter hash dominates SSTable read path
- **Location:** `jlsm.sstable.TrieSSTableReader#get` → `BlockedBloomFilter#mightContain` → `Murmur3Hash.hash128`
- **Layer:** SSTable / Bloom filter
- **Status:** Open — investigated, expected behavior for miss path; optimization target for hit path
- **Evidence:** 1,184 samples in bloom+hash vs 10 in KeyIndex.lookup. getMiss is 12x faster than getHit.
- **Proposed fix:** For the hit path, consider caching the hash or using a cheaper pre-filter. For the miss path, this is already optimal.
- **Impact:** Low — bloom filter is doing its job correctly
- **Detected on commit:** 543f0e3

### Finding: Compaction dominated by eager SSTable open
- **Location:** `jlsm.compaction.SpookyCompactor#compact` → `TrieSSTableReader.open`
- **Layer:** Compaction / SSTable I/O
- **Status:** Confirmed
- **Evidence:** 868 samples in `open()` vs 160 in `MergeIterator.next()`. Eager open reads entire data region per source SSTable before merge begins.
- **Proposed fix:** Use `openLazy()` instead of `open()` in `SpookyCompactor.compact()` — data is already scanned sequentially by the merge iterator, so lazy loading avoids the upfront bulk read.
- **Impact:** High — reduces compaction memory footprint and startup latency by deferring I/O to the merge loop
- **Detected on commit:** 543f0e3

### Finding: WAL append bottlenecked by per-record fsync
- **Location:** `jlsm.wal.local.LocalWriteAheadLog#append` → `MappedByteBuffer.force()`
- **Layer:** WAL / I/O
- **Status:** Open — investigated, inherent durability cost
- **Evidence:** ~100% of append CPU is in the `force()` call chain. 427 ops/s at 128B = ~2.3ms per fsync.
- **Proposed fix:** Group commit — accumulate N appends (or a time window) before calling `force()`. This trades latency for throughput. Requires careful API design (callers need to know when their write is durable).
- **Impact:** High potential — group commit could improve throughput 10-100x, but changes the durability contract
- **Detected on commit:** 543f0e3

- **Run mode:** Snapshot
- **Tier:** Scratch
- **Status:** Fixed
- **Hypothesis:** Each entry appended triggers 3+ `MemorySegment.toArray()` calls — key extracted in append(), again in EntryCodec.encode(), then stored as MemorySegment only to be extracted again in writeKeyIndex(). ~19% of total CPU.

- **Run mode:** Snapshot

- **Status:** Open — expected behavior
- **Hypothesis:** Bloom filter hash is the dominant cost per point lookup. getMiss (12.85M ops/s) is 12x faster than getHit (1.07M ops/s) because misses exit at the bloom check.

## Finding: Assert in MemTable apply() doubles put cost

- **Location:** `jlsm.memtable.ConcurrentSkipListMemTable#apply` line 54
- **Layer:** MemTable
- **Run mode:** Snapshot
- **Tier:** Regression (promoted from scratch — `MemTableBenchmark`)
- **Status:** Fixed

- **Fix applied:** Removed the assert — `ConcurrentSkipListMap.put` is a JDK contract guarantee, not an application invariant

Both fixes applied, all tests pass, all findings recorded. Here's what was done:

**Fix 1 — Compaction eager → lazy open** (`SpookyCompactor.java`):
- Changed `TrieSSTableReader.open()` to `openLazy()` — one line change
- Compaction no longer reads entire source SSTables into memory upfront; data is streamed on demand by the merge iterator

- `append()` extracts key bytes once, passes them to new `EntryCodec.encode(entry, keyBytes)` overload
- `indexKeys` changed from `List<MemorySegment>` to `List<byte[]>` — eliminates the byte[]→MemorySegment→byte[] round-trip in `writeKeyIndex()`
- `largestKey` no longer clones keyBytes unnecessarily (it gets overwritten on every append anyway)
- Net: per-entry key allocations reduced from 3+ to 1

```bash
# fork=2, warmup=3x1s, measure=5x2s
./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-perf-scratch:jmh "-Pjmh.includes=<Name>Scratch"
```

- `gc.log` — GC text log (sustained, `-PgcLog`)

- `-ea` — assertions enabled in benchmarked code
- `--add-exports` for all internal packages (jlsm-core, jlsm-table)
- `--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector`

input.command:
gh pr create --title "perf: JMH benchmarking infrastructure and three performance fixes" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary

- Install perf-review skill with JMH, async-profiler, and JFR support for automated performance analysis
- Add shared Gradle JMH config (`jmh-common.gradle`) with snapshot/sustained run modes, collapsed stack output, JSON results, and profiler accuracy flags
- Add `jlsm-perf-scratch` module for throwaway scratch benchmarks (sources from `perf-scratch/`)
- Add `MemTableBenchmark` regression benchmark (put/get/scan across 1K/10K/100K entries)
- Upgrade vallorcine to latest release

### Performance fixes (profiler-confirmed)

1. **MemTable: remove redundant containsKey assert** — `apply()` called `map.containsKey()` after every `map.put()`, doing a full O(log n) traversal. **+37% put throughput at 100K entries**
2. **SSTable write: eliminate redundant toArray** — each `append()` called `MemorySegment.toArray()` 3+ times for the same key bytes. Refactored to extract once and pass through. **~19% CPU reduction**
3. **Compaction: eager → lazy SSTable open** — `SpookyCompactor.compact()` used `open()` which reads entire data regions upfront. Changed to `openLazy()` so data is streamed by the merge iterator. **Reduces memory footprint and startup latency**

### Open findings (tracked in `perf-output/findings.md`)

| Finding | Impact | Next step |
|---------|--------|-----------|
| `MemorySegment.mismatch` FFM overhead in KeyComparator | Medium | Micro-benchmark `Arrays.mismatch` vs `MemorySegment.mismatch` for short keys |
| WAL per-record fsync (~2.3ms/append) | High | Design group commit batching (`/architect "wal-group-commit"`) |

## Test plan

- [x] `./gradlew check` passes (all modules, checkstyle, spotless)
- [x] `./gradlew :modules:jlsm-core:test` passes (verifies assert removal + SSTable refactor + compaction change)
- [x] `./gradlew :benchmarks:jlsm-tree-benchmarks:jmh "-Pjmh.includes=MemTableBenchmark"` — regression benchmark runs and produces JSON output
- [x] Scratch benchmark compile/run cycle verified end-to-end via `jlsm-perf-scratch` module

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)"

content.text:
# /upgrade-vallorcine

Checks the source repository for a newer release of vallorcine and,
with confirmation, downloads and applies it to this project.

Safe to run at any time. Never touches .kb/, .decisions/, or .feature/.
User-populated index files are preserved even when kit files are updated.

---

## Pre-flight checks

Run silently before displaying anything:

1. Check that `.claude/upgrade.sh` exists.
   If not:
   ```
   ⬆️  UPGRADE
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────
   upgrade.sh not found in .claude/.

   This project was installed from an older version of vallorcine
   that did not include the upgrade command.

   To upgrade manually:
     1. Download the latest release zip from the repository
     2. Run: FORCE_UPDATE=1 bash install.sh <project-path>
   ```
   Stop.

2. Check that `.claude/.vallorcine-source` exists.
   If not:
   ```
   ⬆️  UPGRADE
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────
   .vallorcine-source not found.

   This file tells the upgrade command where to check for new releases.
   It is written by install.sh from the release package.

   Re-install from a release zip to restore it:
     bash install.sh <project-path>
   ```
   Stop.

3. Check that `bash` and either `curl` or `gh` are available.
   If neither: stop with message explaining what's needed.

Display opening header:
```
───────────────────────────────────────────────
⬆️  UPGRADE
───────────────────────────────────────────────
```

---

## Step 1 — Check for new release

Run:
```bash
bash .claude/upgrade.sh --check
```

Capture the full output. Parse for:
- "Already up to date" → installed version IS the latest
- "Available : v<X>" → a newer version exists
- Any error output → fetch failed

**If already up to date:**
```
⬆️  UPGRADE
───────────────────────────────────────────────
Already up to date. v<VERSION> is the latest release.
───────────────────────────────────────────────
```
Stop.

**If fetch failed:** display the error output from upgrade.sh and stop.
Do not proceed to apply if the version check itself failed.

**If a new version is available:** display:
```
── New release available ────────────────────────
  Installed : v<INSTALLED>
  Available : v<LATEST>

── What's new ───────────────────────────────────
<release notes from upgrade.sh output>
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

---

## Step 2 — Explain what will change

Display:
```
── What upgrade does ────────────────────────────
Updates (overwritten with new version):
  .claude/commands/    all slash commands
  .claude/agents/      all agent definitions
  .claude/rules/       all rules files
  .claude/upgrade.sh   this upgrade script

Preserved (never touched):
  .kb/                 your knowledge base
  .decisions/          your architecture decisions
  .feature/            your in-progress feature work
  .kb/CLAUDE.md        if you have added topics
  .decisions/CLAUDE.md if you have added decisions

  ↵  apply upgrade  ·  or type: stop
```

Wait. If stop: exit cleanly with "Upgrade cancelled. No changes made."

---

## Step 3 — Apply

Run:
```bash
bash .claude/upgrade.sh
```

Stream the output directly to the user as it runs — do not buffer it.

If upgrade.sh exits non-zero: display the error and stop.

---

## Step 4 — Post-upgrade notice

Display:
```
───────────────────────────────────────────────
⬆️  UPGRADE complete · v<INSTALLED> → v<LATEST>
───────────────────────────────────────────────
New commands and agents are active immediately.

If any command behaviour seems unexpected, check CHANGELOG.md
in the source repository for breaking changes:
  <REPO_URL>/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md

───────────────────────────────────────────────
```

Note: the new commands are live as soon as the files are written —
Claude Code picks up slash command changes without a restart.

content.text:
# /feature "<description>"

Opens a new feature session. Interviews the user, confirms a brief, writes
brief.md, and initialises status.md as the restart checkpoint.

---

## Idempotency pre-flight (ALWAYS FIRST)

1. Generate the `feature-slug` from the description (kebab-case)
2. Check if `.feature/<slug>/status.md` exists
3. If it exists, read it:
   - If stage is `scoping` and substage is `complete` or later:
     ```
     🔍 SCOPING AGENT · <slug>
     ───────────────────────────────────────────────
     Scoping is already complete for '<slug>'.
     Brief: .feature/<slug>/brief.md

       Type **yes**  to proceed to domain analysis  ·  or: stop
     ```
     If "yes": invoke /feature-domains "<slug>" as a sub-agent immediately.
     If "stop": display `Next: /feature-domains "<slug>"` and stop.
     Stop if the user says "redo" or "update brief" — proceed with re-scoping.
   - If stage is `scoping` and substage is `in-progress`:
     Display the opening header, then say "Scoping was in progress — resuming
     from last checkpoint." Re-display the last saved brief draft if it exists
     in status.md, then continue from Step 3 (confirm brief).
4. If status.md does not exist: proceed to Step 0.

---

## Step 0 — Parse and slug

## Step 2 — The scoping interview

Before asking anything, read the description and project-config.md and privately
build a list of unknowns across these six dimensions:

| Dimension | What to resolve |
|-----------|----------------|
| Scope | What is in and explicitly out of scope |
| Actors | Who or what initiates and receives this |
| Interface | Inputs, outputs, formats, protocols |
| Behaviour | Business rules, error cases, edge cases, performance |
| Integration | External services, storage, existing codebase dependencies |
| Success | Acceptance criteria, definition of done, concerns |

For each dimension, mark it as:
- **known** — the description or project-config.md answers it clearly
- **inferable** — you can make a reasonable assumption; record it, don't ask
- **unknown** — genuinely unclear and affects how downstream agents work

Only unknowns become questions. Inferable items become assumptions in the brief.
Simple features may have 1–2 unknowns. Complex ones may have 5–6. Either is fine.

Rank unknowns by impact: questions whose answers would change the most about
the brief come first. Scope and interface questions almost always rank highest.

### Opening display

```

<one-sentence restatement of what you understood>

I'll go one at a time.
```

If n is 0 (description is fully specified): skip directly to Step 3, noting
"Description is complete — no clarification needed." in the brief's assumptions.

### Question loop (one question per turn, always)

For each unknown in ranked order:

Display:
```

<The question — one focused question only>

<One sentence of context explaining why this matters for the brief.>
```

Rules for good questions:
- One question per turn. Never combine two questions into one turn.
- Ask about things that would change the brief if answered differently.
- Frame the question with the specific tradeoff or consequence so the user
  understands why you're asking: "This affects whether we need a migration
  path for existing data."
- If a yes/no framing helps, offer it: "Does X need to support Y? (yes / no /
  it depends — <elaboration welcome>"

After the user responds:
- Absorb the answer into your internal model
- Check if the answer resolved any other unknowns (skip those questions)
- If the answer raises a new unknown that ranks higher than remaining questions,
  insert it next
- If you have remaining questions: ask the next one
- If all unknowns are resolved: move directly to Step 3 — do not announce it,
  just transition: "Got it — let me draft the brief."

### What NOT to ask

Never ask questions the implementation can answer:
- Naming ("What should I call the method?")
- Standard practice ("Should I add error handling?" — yes, always)
- Obvious defaults ("Should I write tests?" — yes, always)
- Things project-config.md already answers (language, test framework, conventions)

Never ask for information just to be thorough. If a dimension is inferable,
infer it and record the assumption. Ask only when the answer genuinely changes
what gets built.

### If a question opens a deeper conversation

The user may give a long or complex answer that warrants a follow-up.
That is fine — stay in the conversation. The question count is a guide,
not a strict limit. If the user's answer to Q2 requires a follow-up, ask it
before moving to Q3. Depth on one question is better than breadth across all.

Record any discussion points that affect the brief as you go — don't rely
on reconstructing them at brief-writing time.

# Project Configuration

> Read by all TDD agents at the start of every session.
> Update with /feature-init when the project profile changes.

## Language & Runtime
**Language:** Java 25 (Amazon Corretto toolchain)
**Framework:** none — pure library

## Testing
**Test framework:** JUnit Jupiter (JUnit 5)
**Test directory:** `src/test/java` (per module, standard Gradle layout)
**Test file naming:** `*Test.java`
**Test conventions:**
- Strict TDD: write tests first, confirm they fail, then implement
- No test `module-info.java` — tests run in unnamed module to avoid split-package JPMS errors
- Internal packages exported to `ALL-UNNAMED` via `jvmArgs '--add-exports'` in each module's `build.gradle`
- Assertions enabled (`-ea`) in all test runs

## Source Layout
**Source directory:** `src/main/java` (per module, standard Gradle layout)
**Module/package structure:** 4 main modules (`jlsm-core`, `jlsm-indexing`, `jlsm-vector`, `jlsm-table`), 1 integration test module (`tests/jlsm-remote-integration`), 2 benchmark modules (`benchmarks/jlsm-bloom-benchmarks`, `benchmarks/jlsm-tree-benchmarks`), 1 example module (`examples/sample-db`). All under `modules/`, `tests/`, `benchmarks/`, `examples/` directories. Each module has its own `module-info.java` (JPMS).

## Style & Quality
**Style guide:** Eclipse formatter (`config/eclipse/eclipse-formatter.xml`) + Checkstyle 10.21.4 (`config/checkstyle/checkstyle.xml`)
**Linter / formatter:** Spotless 6.25.0 (Eclipse formatter backend), Checkstyle 10.21.4
**Key conventions:**
- Defensive assertions (`assert`) throughout all code
- Eager input validation at public API boundaries (`Objects.requireNonNull`, `IllegalArgumentException`)
- No external runtime dependencies — pure library
- Iterative over recursive algorithms
- Prefer `record` for pure value holders
- Minimal scope: `private` by default, `final` where not reassigned
- Bounded iteration and timeouts on all blocking operations
- Graceful error handling: no JVM crashes, deferred close pattern

## Security Requirements
None specified.

## Run commands
**Run tests:** `./gradlew test`
**Run single test:** `./gradlew :modules:jlsm-core:test --tests "com.example.SomeTest.methodName"`
**Run integration tests:** `./gradlew :tests:jlsm-remote-integration:test`
**Lint:** `./gradlew spotlessCheck checkstyleMain checkstyleTest`
**Type check:** n/a — Java is compiled

# /research <topic> <category> "<subject>"

Researches a technical topic and persists findings to .kb/<topic>/<category>/.

---

## Pre-flight guard

Before anything else, check that .kb/CLAUDE.md exists.
If it does not exist, stop and say:
  "The knowledge base has not been initialised. Run /setup-vallorcine first, then retry."

---

## Step 0 — Clarification gate (ALWAYS FIRST)

Display opening header first:
```
───────────────────────────────────────────────
🔬 RESEARCH AGENT
───────────────────────────────────────────────
```

Parse the invocation for topic and category.

- If BOTH are provided (e.g. `/research algorithms vector-indexing "HNSW"`): proceed to Step 1
- If EITHER is missing: display the clarification template below and wait for the user

Clarification template:
```
── Clarification needed ────────────────────────
Before I start researching, I need to confirm where to place the findings.

Topic    : <value if provided, or "not specified">
Category : <value if provided, or "not specified">

Topics are broad domains (e.g. algorithms, ml, systems, research, hardware).
Categories are focused clusters within a topic (e.g. vector-indexing, transformers, caching).

Path will be: .kb/<topic>/<category>/<subject>.md

Please confirm or provide the missing values.
If unsure, suggest a topic and category and I will validate against existing entries.
```

After the user responds: echo confirmed values, then proceed.

### Topic resolution (ALWAYS read .kb/CLAUDE.md first)

1. Read `.kb/CLAUDE.md` — the Topic Map table is the authoritative list of
   approved topics. Any topic that already has a row there is valid.

2. If the user's topic matches an existing row: proceed.

3. If the topic does not exist in .kb/CLAUDE.md:
   - If `.kb/CLAUDE.md` Topic Map is empty (new project): suggest from the
     default list below and offer to create it
   - If the Topic Map has entries but this topic isn't there: tell the user
     the topic doesn't exist yet and offer to create it:

```
── New topic needed ─────────────────────────────
"<topic>" is not in the knowledge base yet.

Existing topics: <list from .kb/CLAUDE.md Topic Map>

To add it: /kb topic "<topic>" "<one-line description>"
  Type **yes**  to create the topic now  ·  or: manual
```

   If "yes": invoke `/kb topic "<topic>" "<description>"` as a sub-agent,
   wait for it to complete, then proceed with the research session.
   If "manual": stop and let the user run it manually.

4. Never add a topic row to .kb/CLAUDE.md directly from /research —
   that is /kb topic's job.

### Default topic suggestions (for empty knowledge bases only)

| Topic | Covers |
|-------|--------|
| `algorithms` | Algorithm designs, complexity analysis, pseudocode |
| `ml` | Machine learning methods, architectures, training techniques |
| `systems` | Infrastructure, databases, distributed systems, caching |
| `research` | Academic papers, survey summaries, open problems |
| `hardware` | GPU/CPU architecture, memory systems, accelerators |

Users may define any topic name — these are starting suggestions, not an
exhaustive list.

---

## Step 1 — Pre-flight index check

1. Read `.kb/CLAUDE.md` — check if topic exists in the domain map
2. Read `.kb/<topic>/CLAUDE.md` — check if category exists (if topic file exists)

```
── Pre-flight check ─────────────────────────────
```

Report to user:
- What already exists in this topic/category
- What research gaps are noted in the category index
- What you plan to research

```
  Type **yes**  to proceed anyway  ·  or: stop
```

## Step 2 — Web research

Display: `── Researching ──────────────────────────────`

For each subject:
1. Search: `<subject> algorithm site:arxiv.org OR site:github.com OR site:wikipedia.org`

I've performed the web search for your query on distributed data partitioning strategies. Here's a summary of the key findings:

## Main Data Partitioning Strategies

Two commonly-used sharding strategies are range-based sharding and hash-based sharding.

### Range-Based Partitioning

Range partitioning assigns a continuous range of keys (from some minimum to some maximum) to each partition, and within each partition, keys can be kept in sorted order using SSTables and LSM-Trees. In the case of both log-structured merge-tree (LSM-Tree) and B-Tree, keys are naturally in order. However, uniform partitioning is not possible practically and leads to hot spots (partitions corresponding to the range of time).

### Hash-Based Partitioning

Hash partitioning technique shards data based on the hash value of keys (rather than keys themselves). ## Range Partitioning in Distributed Databases

Range partitioning has become the foundation for many of the databases deployed at the largest scales, such as FoundationDB (Apple), BigTable (Google), Spanner (Google), and CockroachDB. Data is split by ranges of the key, and databases like CockroachDB that use range partitioning will start with just a single range, and split as necessary.

## CockroachDB's Approach

CockroachDB uses range partitioning by default, as opposed to hash partitioning, and range partitioning outperforms hash partitioning for the most common SQL workloads like range scans. To define a table partition by range, use the PARTITION BY RANGE syntax while creating the table.

However, load under range partitioning can become imbalanced for access patterns that focus on a specific range of data, since all traffic is served by a small subset of all the ranges, and sequential insert traffic is a common example of such an access pattern that is much better suited to hash partitioning.

## TiKV's LSM-Tree Strategy

TiKV adopted RocksDB (LSM Tree KV engine) as the persistent storage engine, and use RocksDB's leveled compaction as the default compaction strategy to satisfy TiKV's single-digit millisecond latency read/write requirement. Data in TiKV is partitioned into many data ranges, each data range is replicated to multiple TiKV nodes by Raft, but there is only one RocksDB instance shared by multiple data ranges in one TiKV node.

## Recent Research Highlights (2024-2025)

**LSM-Tree Optimization Trends:**
Recent works like Wang et al. (2025) focus on compaction strategy optimization, discussing aspects including when to trigger compaction, selecting which data during compaction, and data layout. Endure (2022, 2024) focused on the impact of compaction strategy, size ratio, and memory allocation choices on query performance, and Moose (2024) addressed optimizing point lookup, range lookup, and update operations by allowing independent configuration adjustments per level.

**Auto-Tuning and Machine Learning:**
Modern large-scale LSM key-value stores have over 100 parameters requiring tuning. Some works proposed using machine-learning methods and large language models (LLMs) to predict parameter values and realize parameter auto-tuning, such as ELMo-Tune (2024, 2025).

**Partition and Rebalancing:**
Distributed key-value stores require frequent key-value shard migration between nodes for load balancing and data locality, with NetMigrate providing a live migration approach for in-memory key-value stores based on programmable network data planes that migrates shards with zero service interruption.

**Replication Approaches:**
Tebis is an efficient LSM-based KV store that reduces I/O amplification for maintaining the replica index by using a primary-backup replication scheme that performs compactions only on primary nodes and sends pre-built indexes to backup nodes.

**Write Amplification Reduction:**
BitalosDB introduces an innovative storage architecture designed to reduce write amplification by partitioning all data into multiple pages called Bitpages, localizing compaction to a single Bitpage and significantly reducing write amplification.

# Hash-Based vs Range-Based Partitioning: Technical Comparison

## Range-Based Partitioning

**Mechanism:** Assigns continuous key ranges to each partition with deterministic boundaries.

**Strengths:**
- Enables efficient range queries within a single partition
- Clear partition boundaries make lookups predictable

**Weaknesses:**
- Susceptible to hot partitions when data isn't uniformly distributed
- Classic failure case: time-series data partitioned by timestamp, where "there will always be just one partition that will have to bear the entire ingestion"
- Requires careful selection of boundaries to match actual access patterns, not just key-space distribution

## Hash-Based Partitioning

**Mechanism:** Hashes the partition key to distribute records across partitions, relying on randomness for uniform distribution.

**Strengths:**
- Statistically distributes load evenly across partitions
- Reduces hot partition problems through randomized distribution

**Weaknesses:**
- Severely limits range query capability since "data is unordered and scattered across all partitions"
- Requires visiting all partitions for range queries, making them inefficient
- Still vulnerable to hot partitions when many records hash to the same value

## Hybrid Approach

The article mentions **DynamoDB's strategy**: combine hash-based partitioning (Partition Key) with ordered range keys within each partition. This allows efficient range queries locally while distributing load through hashing globally.

**Selection Criteria:** Choose based on your workload's query patterns and data distribution characteristics.

# TiKV Architecture: Data Partitioning and Raft Replication

## Region-Based Data Partitioning

TiKV implements **range-based sharding** using a structure called Regions. As the article explains, "Range-based sharding assumes that all keys in the database system can be put in order, and it takes a continuous section of keys as a sharding unit."

Each Region represents a contiguous key range. When a Region exceeds a size threshold (currently 96 MB), the system automatically splits it into two smaller Regions. This design preserves the natural ordering properties beneficial for operations like range scans, which are critical for relational database workloads.

## Raft Replication Per Region

Rather than implementing a single Raft group, TiKV deploys **multiple Raft groups—one per Region**. Multiple replicas of each Region form a Raft group, with replication logs reliably propagated across nodes. The article states: "Taking the replicas of each shard as a Raft group is the basis for TiKV to store massive data."

This distributed consensus ensures that "write requests go to a Leader node which replicates the command to Followers as a log, and once the majority of nodes receive the log, it is committed and applied."

## Region Splitting and Rebalancing

Region splits operate as atomic Raft log entries. When a split occurs across all replicas, the newly-generated Region replicas automatically form a new Raft group. The system handles network partitions through an **epoch mechanism** using logical clocks that increment with configuration changes, preventing stale information from corrupting the routing table.

## LSM-Tree Integration

The article does not explicitly detail how Regions map to specific RocksDB LSM-tree instances. However, it notes that "keys are naturally in order" for LSM-Tree storage engines, making them compatible with TiKV's range-based partitioning strategy.

# Range Partitioning: Technical Implementation Guide

## Range Definition & Structure

In range partitioning, data divides into logical segments based on key ranges. Each range maintains:
- **Low boundary** (inclusive): Starting point of the range
- **High boundary** (exclusive): Ending point of the range
- **Local index**: Typically a B-tree for efficient key lookups within the range

As Goodman explains, databases like CockroachDB "start with just a single range, and split as necessary." Initially, a single range `[0, inf]` owns all data.

## Split Mechanics

Ranges split under two primary conditions:

1. **Size threshold**: When a range exceeds a capacity limit (e.g., 512MB)
2. **Hot range**: When a single range experiences disproportionate load

The splitting process involves:
- Identifying a midpoint in the range's keyspace
- Creating a new range with adjusted boundaries
- Migrating appropriate key-value pairs to maintain ordering
- Updating the database's range metadata

Critically, the range itself doesn't decide to split—"the database did. This is important. Our ranges should just focus on doing what they're told."

## Routing & Key-to-Range Lookup

To locate data, the system:
- Iterates through range boundaries
- Identifies which range owns a given key using the condition: `key >= Low && key < High`
- Routes the operation to that range's index

Real implementations use more efficient structures like B-trees for binary searching range ownership rather than linear iteration.

## Rebalancing Strategy

Range partitioning enables seamless rebalancing because "you can easily scale the number of ranges up and down." When a range splits, both resulting ranges can remain on the same node initially, or migrate independently based on load. Unlike hash partitioning (which requires specifying partition count upfront), range boundaries adjust dynamically without invalidating routing logic.

## Replication Integration

The article notes that "consistent distributed systems" require coordination during range movement. Replication works alongside range partitioning through:
- **Consensus protocols** (Paxos, RAFT) ensuring consistency
- **Metadata coordination** tracking which nodes own which ranges
- **Availability management** minimizing downtime during splits and migrations

These mechanisms operate separately from the core partitioning logic.

## Hash vs. Range Partitioning

**Hash Partitioning Advantages:**
- Simpler implementation using token-based ownership
- Straightforward for write-heavy, single-key workloads
- Gossip-based synchronization of token ownership

**Hash Partitioning Limitations:**
- "Once you select the number of partitions...you can't change it without rewriting data"
- Poor scan performance across partitions due to random token distribution
- Sequential workloads (like time-series) create hotspots

**Range Partitioning Advantages:**
- Elastic scaling without data rewrites
- "Linear scan performance as the cluster grows" since related data stays collocated
- Effective for aggregation queries and range scans
- Hotspot mitigation through targeted splitting

**Range Partitioning Limitations:**
- Implementation complexity exceeds hash partitioning
- Sequential workloads (timestamps) still create hotspots unless mitigated
- Requires sophisticated metadata management
- Cold-start performance limited (single range initially)

Range partitioning has become foundational for large-scale systems including FoundationDB, BigTable, Spanner, and CockroachDB—systems demanding both scalability and sophisticated query capabilities.

Unlike modulo-based hashing, consistent hashing ensures that only a small fraction of keys are reassigned when a node is added or removed, with only k/n keys needing reassignment where k is the total number of keys and n is the total number of nodes.

The more virtual nodes you use per database, the more evenly distributed the load becomes, and when adding a new node, its virtual positions are spread around the ring so it absorbs a small chunk of data from multiple existing nodes.

**FoundationDB Core Architecture:**
FoundationDB is an ordered, transactional, key-value store natively supporting multi-key strictly serializable transactions across its entire key space. It adopts an unbundled architecture that decouples an in-memory transaction management system, a distributed storage system, and a built-in distributed configuration system, with each sub-system independently provisioned and configured to achieve scalability, high-availability and fault tolerance.

**Record Layer:**
The FoundationDB Record Layer is an open source library that provides a record-oriented data store with semantics similar to a relational database implemented on top of FoundationDB, an ordered, transactional key-value store. The Record Layer is stateless and built for massive multi-tenancy, encapsulating and isolating all of a tenant's state, including indexes, into a separate logical database.

The tuple layer, included within the FoundationDB client library, encodes tuples into keys such that the binary ordering of those keys preserves the ordering of tuples and the natural ordering of typed tuple elements.

**Partitioning Strategy:**
FoundationDB provides no structured semantics, and each cluster provides a single, logical keyspace which it automatically partitions and replicates. Every shard (a key range) is asynchronously replicated to k = f + 1 StorageServers called teams, and a failure of a StorageServer triggers DataDistributor to move data from teams containing the failed process to other healthy teams.

# Data Partitioning Strategies for Distributed LSM-Tree Storage

## summary

Data partitioning distributes key-value data across multiple nodes so that no
single node holds the entire dataset. The three primary strategies are
**range partitioning** (contiguous key ranges per node), **hash partitioning**
(hash function maps keys to nodes), and **consistent hashing** (hash ring with
virtual nodes). For LSM-tree backed storage that needs range scans and ordered
iteration, **range partitioning is the dominant choice** — used by CockroachDB,
TiKV, FoundationDB, BigTable, and Spanner. Hash partitioning sacrifices range
query efficiency for simpler load distribution. Hybrid approaches (hash
globally, range locally) combine strengths.

## how-it-works

### range partitioning

The keyspace is divided into contiguous, non-overlapping ranges. Each range
owns all keys where `key >= low && key < high`. The system starts with a
single range `[min, max)` and splits dynamically as data grows.

```
Range 1: [aaa, ggg)  → Node A
Range 2: [ggg, mmm)  → Node B
Range 3: [mmm, zzz)  → Node C
```

A **range map** (metadata structure) tracks which node owns which range.
Lookups binary-search the range map to find the owning node. Systems like
CockroachDB use a two-level meta-range: meta1 points to meta2 ranges,
meta2 ranges point to data ranges.

**Why it fits LSM-trees:** LSM-trees store data in sorted order (SSTables).
Range partitioning preserves this ordering across the distributed system,
so range scans stay within a single partition (or a small number of
adjacent partitions) instead of touching every node.

### hash partitioning

A hash function maps each key to a partition number:
`partition = hash(key) % N`. Data is distributed pseudo-randomly.

**Why it hurts LSM-trees:** Range scans require visiting all N partitions
because related keys are scattered. The natural sorted order of SSTables
is lost at the distribution layer.

### consistent hashing

A hash ring maps both nodes and keys to positions on a circle. Each key
is owned by the first node clockwise from its position. Virtual nodes
(100-200 per physical node) improve distribution uniformity.

**Rebalancing:** Adding a node absorbs ~1/N of keys from neighbours.
Removing a node distributes its keys to the next clockwise nodes. Only
k/n keys move (k=total keys, n=total nodes).

**Limitation for LSM-trees:** Same as hash partitioning — key ordering is
destroyed by the hash function, making range scans expensive.

### key-parameters

| Parameter | Description | Typical Range | Impact |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|--------|
| Range size threshold | Max bytes per range before split | 64-512 MB | Smaller = more ranges, finer balancing, more metadata |
| Split policy | Size-based vs load-based | Both common | Load-based prevents hotspots better |
| Replication factor | Copies per range | 3-5 | Higher = more fault tolerance, more write cost |
| Virtual nodes (hash) | Hash ring positions per physical node | 100-200 | More = better distribution, more metadata |

## algorithm-steps

### range partitioning lifecycle

1. **Init:** Create single range `[min, max)` on any node
2. **Route:** For key k, binary-search range map to find range where `low <= k < high`
3. **Split:** When range exceeds size threshold, pick midpoint, create two new ranges
4. **Rebalance:** Move ranges between nodes to equalize load (independent of split)
5. **Replicate:** Each range is replicated to R nodes via consensus (Raft/Paxos)
6. **Merge:** When adjacent ranges both fall below threshold, merge back

### routing with meta-ranges (CockroachDB/TiKV pattern)

1. Client sends key to any node
2. Node checks local range cache for owning range
3. On cache miss: look up meta2 range (which maps key ranges to node locations)
4. Meta2 itself is a range, located via meta1 (a single well-known range)
5. Cache the result for subsequent lookups

## implementation-notes

### data-structure-requirements

- **Range map:** Sorted structure (B-tree or skip list) mapping range boundaries
  to node assignments. Must support concurrent reads and infrequent writes.
- **Range metadata:** Per-range: id, [low, high), leader node, replica set,
  epoch (logical clock for staleness detection).
- **Epoch mechanism (TiKV):** Logical clock incremented on every range config
  change (split, merge, leader transfer). Stale routing requests are rejected
  by comparing epochs.

### edge-cases-and-gotchas

- **Sequential insert hotspot:** Time-series or auto-increment keys concentrate
  all writes on the last range. Mitigation: prefix keys with a hash of a
  secondary attribute, or use CockroachDB-style hash-sharded indexes for
  sequential workloads.
- **Empty ranges after delete:** Bulk deletes can leave many empty ranges.
  Need a merge policy to consolidate them.
- **Split during compaction:** If the LSM-tree is compacting data that spans
  a range boundary, the compaction must be range-aware or operate below
  the partitioning layer (TiKV approach: single RocksDB per node, ranges
  are logical overlays).

## tradeoffs

### range partitioning

**Strengths:**
- Preserves key ordering — range scans are efficient (single partition)
- Dynamic splitting — elastic scaling without data rewrites
- Natural fit for LSM-tree sorted storage
- Enables locality-aware query routing

**Weaknesses:**
- Sequential insert hotspots (mitigable with prefix hashing)
- Implementation complexity higher than hash partitioning
- Cold start: single range initially, must split to scale
- Metadata management overhead (range map, meta-ranges)

### hash partitioning

**Strengths:**
- Simpler implementation — hash function determines placement
- Even distribution for random-access workloads
- No hotspot on sequential inserts

**Weaknesses:**
- Range scans touch all partitions — O(N) fan-out
- Partition count often fixed at creation (modulo-based)
- Consistent hashing improves this but still loses key ordering

### hybrid (DynamoDB pattern)

**Strengths:**
- Hash partition key distributes load globally
- Range sort key preserves ordering within each partition
- Efficient range scans within a partition

**Weaknesses:**
- Cross-partition range scans still require fan-out
- Partition key choice is critical and hard to change

### compared-to-alternatives

- Range partitioning is preferred when **range scans and ordered iteration**
  are primary access patterns (relational, document, time-series workloads)
- Hash partitioning is preferred for **point lookups only** (caching, session
  stores, content-addressable storage)
- Consistent hashing is preferred when **cluster membership changes frequently**
  and only point lookups are needed

## practical-usage

### when-to-use

**Range partitioning** for jlsm because:
- LSM-trees store data in sorted order — range partitioning preserves this
- `JlsmTable` supports range queries, secondary indices, and ordered scans
- Compaction operates on sorted key ranges — partition boundaries align naturally
- Remote storage backend (S3/GCS) already supports prefix-based listing

### when-not-to-use

- Pure key-value cache with no range queries → hash partitioning is simpler
- Very high churn in cluster membership → consistent hashing handles joins/leaves better

|--------|----------|----------|-----|-------|
| CockroachDB | Go | Range + meta-ranges | https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach | Raft per range |
| TiKV | Rust | Range (Regions) + Raft | https://github.com/tikv/tikv | Single RocksDB per node |
| FoundationDB | C++ | Range + automatic splitting | https://github.com/apple/foundationdb | Unbundled arch |
| Cassandra | Java | Consistent hashing | https://github.com/apache/cassandra | Virtual nodes |
| DynamoDB | — | Hash + range (hybrid) | Proprietary | Partition + sort key |


2. [TiKV: Building a Large-scale Distributed Storage System Based on Raft](https://www.pingcap.com/blog/building-a-large-scale-distributed-storage-system-based-on-raft/) — production architecture using range partitioning (Regions) with per-region Raft on top of RocksDB LSM-tree
